source.title: A Simple Recipe for Contrastively Pre-Training Video-First Encoders Beyond 16 Frames
source.authors: Pinelopi Papalampidi; Skanda Koppula; Shreya Pathak; Justin Chiu; Joseph Heyward; Viorica Patraucean; Jiajun Shen; Antoine Miech; A. Zisserman; Aida Nematzdeh

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present; no apparent garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: Compares downstream video-captioning scores at two frozen language-model sizes, a different measure and setup from the language-model pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fit power laws, test extrapolation from smaller runs, or estimate compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. The relevant results are the Table 2 zero-shot CIDEr comparisons for 400M versus 1B frozen language models. Other architecture, masking, frame-count, and memory results do not test the versions' named scaling-law measures.
record.test_reason: This is a video-encoder recipe paper about memory-efficient contrastive pre-training (masking, attention types, adapters). It fits no scaling-law curves and reports no held-out pretraining loss. The only size comparison is an incidental two-point swap of a frozen, separately pretrained decoder (400M vs 1B) inside a video-to-text system, with only adapter layers trained. That is not a test of whether language-model downstream performance improves predictably with scale: two points cannot show predictability, and the system is a vision–language pipeline, not a language model scaled in pretraining. Hoffmann et al. (Chinchilla) is cited only as the LLM used to summarise ASR transcripts. I record the finding under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but misplaced in emphasis. The authors' main conclusion is that masking up to 75% of video tokens during contrastive pre-training gives 2-3x memory savings with little performance loss. This lets video-first encoders scale to 256 frames (4.3 min), and LongViViT then beats LLM-assisted modular methods on YouCook2 and EgoSchema. The 400M→1B frozen-LM result is a side remark of 'moderate improvements'. The authors draw no conclusions about scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares downstream video-captioning CIDEr scores for two frozen decoder sizes, rather than measuring held-out language-model pretraining loss across parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect of changing the frozen LM size varies by dataset and video-model variant; two comparisons show lower scores at 1B.

fits_no_version.finding: Swapping the frozen LM decoder from 400M to 1B in a video-to-text system changes zero-shot CIDEr by -0.6 to +2.0 points across 4 benchmarks and 3 encoders. Ten of 12 cells rise; the authors call these 'moderate improvements'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger frozen language decoders give small, inconsistent gains in zero-shot video captioning when only adapter layers are trained.

record.problems: Only one 400M-to-1B decoder-size comparison is reported for the relevant downstream metric; there is no broad scale range or uncertainty estimate, and outcomes are not uniformly increasing.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results pertinent to the tested V6 comparison were left out.

untested.parts: No pretraining-loss sweeps over parameters, tokens or compute.
No fits on small runs and no extrapolation.
Architecture comparisons use retrieval or captioning metrics on video encoders, not LM loss at fixed parameters.
Video models are trained, but no power-law form is fitted for any modality or regime.
Only a two-point frozen-decoder swap in a video-to-text system; no scaling curve and no loss-to-task relation.
No exponents or fitting choices are examined.

record.verdict_notes: Encoder size scaling (ViT-B to ViT-L, Figure 3) and memory scaling (Figure 11) report only memory use or efficiency-method drops, not loss or performance scaling, so none bears on any version.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweeps over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run loss fits or predictions of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token counts.
Architecture comparisons use downstream retrieval or captioning metrics, not held-out loss at fixed parameter count.
Although the study trains video models, it does not test whether a power-law loss form holds for video or other training regimes.

Tests only zero-shot video-captioning CIDEr when changing the frozen LM from 400M to 1B; it does not test a predictable curve across a broad scale range or performance as a function of pretraining loss.
No analysis of scaling-law exponents, fitting choices, or deviations from power-law loss curves.
